topic: What if you could see one minute ahead?
title: WHAT IF YOU COULD
GLIMPSE ONE MINUTE AHEAD?

power.rule: see exactly sixty seconds into the future, any time you want
power.look: a cyan selection box with marching ants draws around the future moment; a GLIMPSE chip pulses; the frame holds a ghost image of what's coming

script.text: Coffee tips. Glimpse. You catch it.
Bus pulls off. Glimpse. You make it.
Friend speaks. Glimpse. You said it first.
Phone buzzes. Glimpse. It's mum. You let it ring.
What if you could glimpse one minute ahead?
Sounds amazing. Honestly, it does. You win every argument. You dodge every puddle. You ace every test. You're basically a wizard.

script.beat: 4 the turn: the cost, two real facts and the sum
script.text: But here's the catch. A glimpse isn't free. Your brain is two percent of your body weight, and it burns a fifth of all your energy. Twenty watts, nonstop. About a dim light bulb. Now run a whole minute of life in one second. Every single time you glimpse. Sixty times the power. Twelve hundred watts. A space heater, running inside your skull. That's real.

script.beat: 5-7 the cost bites, folded into a question
script.text: At first, a headache. A dull, pounding one. Then the world stutters. Like a video that won't load. Then the glimpses won't stop. One after another after another. Your head is hot. Your vision is white. Your ears are ringing. So what happens when the power fails?

science.claim: Your brain is two percent of your body, and burns a fifth of your energy.
science.working: The adult brain weighs about 1.4 kg of roughly 70 kg of body weight (about 2%), yet uses about 20% of the body's resting energy.
science.source: Raichle & Gusnard, 'Appraising the brain's energy budget', PNAS 2002

science.claim: Twenty watts, nonstop. Run a minute of life in one second: sixty times the power, twelve hundred watts. A space heater inside your skull.
science.working: The brain runs on about 20 W (about 20% of a ~100 W resting body). Assumption for the premise: living 60 seconds in 1 second takes 60 times the work, so 60 x 20 W = 1,200 W. A typical space heater draws 750 to 1,500 W. The 60x is the episode's back-of-envelope assumption, not a measurement.
science.source: Raichle & Gusnard, PNAS 2002 (about 20 W); typical space heater ratings 750-1,500 W
